alignment.note: The Greek presents the deictic interjection ἰδού ('behold'), a Markan narrative intensifier; neither the Peshitta nor the Vulgate render an equivalent particle here, smoothing the introduction of the new character into the prefixed conjunction of the verb.
Note: the Syriac ܘܐܬܐ fuses the conjunction and verb 'and he came'; ἔρχεται / venit.

Greek εἷς ('one') and Syriac ܚܕ ('one') are numeral substantives functioning partitively, whereas the Vulgate quidam ('a certain one') employs the indefinite pronoun — a stylistically idiomatic Latin rendering of the partitive numeral.

Greek τῶν ἀρχισυναγώγων and Latin (de) archisynagogis transmit the compound noun 'synagogue-rulers' as a single lexeme in the genitive/ablative plural, while the Syriac analytically renders it as a construct chain ܪܒܝ ܟܢܘܫܬܐ ('chiefs of the assembly'), reflecting the lack of a single Syriac equivalent for the Greek compound.

Greek ὀνόματι is a dative of respect ('by name') and Latin nomine an ablative of specification, whereas the Syriac ܕܫܡܗ uses a relative-possessive construction ('whose name [was]'), a typical Semitic periphrasis for naming.
Greek καί and Latin et are coordinating, while the Syriac ܘܟܕ fuses the conjunction with the temporal subordinator 'and when'.

Greek ἰδών (aorist participle) and Latin videns (present participle) are circumstantial participles, while the Syriac ܚܙܝܗܝ is a finite perfect verb governed by the preceding 'when' (ܟܕ), a standard Syriac substitution of a temporal clause for a Greek participle.
The object pronoun αὐτόν / eum is incorporated as the enclitic suffix -ܗܝ on the Syriac verb ܚܙܝܗܝ.

Greek πίπτει stands in the vivid historic present, and Latin procidit (a compound 'falls down') likewise present, whereas the Syriac ܢܦܠ is a perfect/past form, the versions normalising Mark's characteristic present-tense narration.
Greek τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ and Latin pedes ejus express 'his feet' analytically, while the Syriac ܪܓܠܘܗܝ compresses noun and possessive into a single suffixed form.
